paragraphs.heading: The deepest trench
paragraphs.text: The Mariana Trench is the deepest ocean trench on Earth. It lies in the western Pacific about 200 km east of the Mariana Islands, and is a crescent about 2,550 km long and 69 km wide. Its deepest known point, 10,935 ± 6 m down, lies in the Challenger Deep, a small slot-shaped valley in its floor, at that valley's southern end. That spot is more than 2 km farther from sea level than the top of Mount Everest.

paragraphs.heading: Crushing and cold
paragraphs.text: At the bottom, the water overhead presses with 1,086 bar, roughly 1,071.8 times normal air pressure at sea level, or eight tons on every square inch. The water there is 1 to 4 °C. Life is still present: Scripps researchers found single-celled organisms called monothalamea 10.6 km down, a record depth. Data also suggest that microbes thrive in the trench.

paragraphs.heading: How it formed
paragraphs.text: Two tectonic plates meet here, along a boundary called the Izu–Bonin–Mariana subduction system. There the western edge of the Pacific plate is thrust under the smaller Mariana plate to its west, a process called subduction. That edge is some of the oldest ocean crust on Earth, up to 170 million years old, so it is cooler and denser, hence the great height difference with the younger Mariana plate. Water locked in minerals of the sinking Pacific plate is released, which melts the upper mantle and creates the volcanic Mariana Islands.

paragraphs.heading: Name and protection
paragraphs.text: The trench takes its name from the nearby Mariana Islands, which honor the Spanish queen Mariana of Austria under the name Las Marianas. The islands sit on the Mariana plate, on the western side of the trench. In 2009 the United States made the parts of the trench inside its exclusive economic zone into the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument. The Challenger Deep is left out, as it lies in the zone of the Federated States of Micronesia.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the depth
paragraphs.text: The Challenger expedition found the trench in 1875 by lowering a weighted rope, which recorded 8,184 m. In 1899 USS Nero measured 9,636 m. In 1951 Challenger II used echo sounding, far more precise and much easier than ropes, and recorded 10,900 m at the spot now called the Challenger Deep. In 1957 the Soviet ship Vityaz reported 11,034 m at a place it called the Mariana Hollow.

paragraphs.heading: Going to the bottom
paragraphs.text: By 2022 there had been 22 crewed and seven uncrewed descents. The first was the bathyscaphe Trieste, which carried Don Walsh and Jacques Piccard to the bottom on 23 January 1960, using gasoline for buoyancy and iron shot as ballast. Its instruments read 11,521 m, later revised to 10,916 m. The uncrewed vehicles Kaikō and Nereus followed in 1996 and 2009, and film director James Cameron made the fourth descent on 26 March 2012.
